--- title: "Training a network" description: "Three settings decide how well a network trains: the learning rate, when to stop, and the random starting weights. Watching the loss on training and validation data shows how to choose each one." order: 3 categories: [neural-networks, optimisation, tuning] --- ## Three settings decide how well a network trains Backpropagation gives every weight its slope, and gradient descent walks downhill. How well the walk ends depends on three settings the data cannot choose: how long each step is, how long to keep walking, and where the walk starts. This page shows what each one does to the same small network, and how to choose it by watching the loss. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.diagram} ![Three training settings: the learning rate sets the length of each step, validation error says when to stop, and the random starting weights decide which valley the walk ends in.](img/training-settings.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Learning rate, step size: a U-shaped loss curve with two walks down it, short steps that settle at the bottom and long steps that jump from side to side; too small crawls, too large overshoots. When to stop, early stopping: two curves of error against training steps, training error falling all the way and validation error falling then rising, with a dashed line at its lowest point; keep the weights where validation error is lowest. Random start, the seed: a wavy loss curve with two valleys and two starting points, each rolling into a different valley; different starts end in different valleys."} ::: The learning rate and the number of steps are hyperparameters, chosen like the node size on [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd). The starting weights are random, so they are not chosen at all; what matters is how much they change the result. All the inputs are standardised first. [Gradient descent](../04-how-algorithms-learn/gradient-descent.qmd) showed that inputs in their measured units make the walk many times longer, because the step has to suit the steepest direction. A network has one learning rate for all its weights, so it needs standardised inputs even more: put `step_normalize()` in every network's recipe. ## Worked example The network is the one from [Forward propagation and backpropagation](forward-and-backward.qmd): depth, temperature and chlorophyll, standardised, predict abundance on a log scale through one hidden layer of tanh units. This time 200 stations are held back as validation data, so we can watch the network on stations it is not fitted to. `train()` now records the loss on both sets at every step. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() model_data <- survey |> select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3) |> drop_na() X <- cbind(depth = as.numeric(scale(model_data$depth_m)), temperature = as.numeric(scale(model_data$temperature_c)), chlorophyll = as.numeric(scale(log1p(model_data$chlorophyll_mg_m3)))) y <- log1p(model_data$abundance) set.seed(20) validation <- sample(nrow(X), 200) X_train <- X[-validation, ]; y_train <- y[-validation] X_valid <- X[validation, ]; y_valid <- y[validation] # The same network and passes as on Forward propagation and backpropagation initialise <- function(seed, n_hidden) { set.seed(seed) list(W1 = matrix(rnorm(ncol(X) * n_hidden, 0, 0.5), ncol(X), n_hidden), b1 = rep(0, n_hidden), w2 = rnorm(n_hidden, 0, 0.5), b2 = mean(y_train)) } forward <- function(par, X) { A1 <- tanh(sweep(X %*% par$W1, 2, par$b1, "+")) list(A1 = A1, prediction = as.numeric(A1 %*% par$w2 + par$b2)) } loss <- function(par, X, y) mean((y - forward(par, X)$prediction)^2) backward <- function(par, X, y) { f <- forward(par, X) d_prediction <- -2 * (y - f$prediction) / nrow(X) d_Z1 <- outer(d_prediction, par$w2) * (1 - f$A1^2) list(W1 = t(X) %*% d_Z1, b1 = colSums(d_Z1), w2 = as.numeric(t(f$A1) %*% d_prediction), b2 = sum(d_prediction)) } # Gradient descent on the training stations, scoring both sets after every step train <- function(par, learning_rate, steps) { training <- validation <- numeric(steps) for (step in seq_len(steps)) { gradient <- backward(par, X_train, y_train) for (nm in names(par)) { par[[nm]] <- par[[nm]] - learning_rate * gradient[[nm]] } training[step] <- loss(par, X_train, y_train) validation[step] <- loss(par, X_valid, y_valid) } list(par = par, training = training, validation = validation) } linear_mse <- mean(resid(lm(y_train ~ X_train))^2) ``` ::: Linear regression on the same three inputs has a training mean squared error of 0.680 on the 541 training stations, the mark every run below has to beat. ### The learning rate trades speed for stability Five networks with four hidden units start from the same weights and differ only in the learning rate. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rates <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 2) sweeps <- map_dfr(rates, \(rate) { run <- train(initialise(3, 4), rate, steps = 1500) tibble(rate, step = seq_along(run$training), mse = run$training) }) rate_summary <- sweeps |> summarise(`Passes linear regression at step` = which(mse < linear_mse)[1], `Lowest training MSE` = round(min(mse, na.rm = TRUE), 3), `Final training MSE` = round(last(mse), 3), .by = rate) |> mutate(rate = as.character(rate)) |> rename(`Learning rate` = rate) rate_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Learning rate | Passes linear regression at step| Lowest training MSE| Final training MSE| |:-------------|--------------------------------:|-------------------:|------------------:| |0.01 | 1122| 0.678| 0.678| |0.05 | 225| 0.595| 0.595| |0.2 | 56| 0.572| 0.572| |0.5 | 23| 0.584| 0.596| |2 | NA| 1.016| NaN|
::: ::: The larger the rate, the sooner the network overtakes linear regression: at step 1,122 with a rate of 0.01, and at step 23 with 0.5. Speed is not everything, though. At 0.5 the steps are too long to settle: the run reaches 0.584, then bounces around the valley floor and ends at 0.596. A rate of 0.2 goes lowest, to 0.572. At 2 every step overshoots further than the last: the loss passes 1,000 at step 6 and becomes `NaN`, R's "not a number", at step 147, with no error or warning. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sweeps |> filter(rate < 2) |> mutate(rate = factor(rate)) |> ggplot(aes(step, mse, colour = rate)) + geom_hline(yintercept = linear_mse, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#9aa5ad") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + annotate("text", x = 1, y = linear_mse, label = "Linear regression", hjust = 0, vjust = 1.6, size = 3.3, colour = "#77818a") + scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000), labels = scales::label_comma()) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.5, 0.9)) + labs(x = "Gradient-descent step (log scale)", y = "Training mean squared error", colour = "Learning rate") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Training loss at four learning rates from the same starting weights, with the steps on a log scale. The dashed line is linear regression. The run at a rate of 2 became NaN and is left out.](training-a-network_files/figure-html/fig-rates-1.png){#fig-rates fig-alt='Four curves of training mean squared error against gradient-descent steps on a log scale from 1 to 1,500, all starting near 1.0. The rate 0.01 curve declines slowly and crosses the dashed linear-regression line at 0.68 only at step 1,122. The rate 0.05 curve crosses it at step 225 and ends at 0.595. The rate 0.2 curve crosses at step 56 and ends lowest, at 0.572. The rate 0.5 curve drops earliest, crossing at step 23, then throws tall narrow spikes and ends in a jagged band at 0.596.' width=1500} ::: ::: Choose the learning rate like any other hyperparameter, trying values a few times apart, and look at the curve as well as the final number: a jagged curve says the rate is too high even when the final score looks good. ### Early stopping keeps the weights with the lowest validation error This network has 40 hidden units for 541 training stations, far more than it needs, and trains for 8,000 steps. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} big <- train(initialise(5, 40), learning_rate = 0.05, steps = 8000) best_step <- which.min(big$validation) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(step = seq_along(big$training), Training = big$training, Validation = big$validation) |> pivot_longer(-step, names_to = "set", values_to = "mse") |> ggplot(aes(step, mse, colour = set)) + geom_vline(xintercept = best_step, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#9aa5ad") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + annotate("text", x = best_step, y = 0.95, hjust = 1, size = 3.3, colour = "#77818a", label = paste0("Lowest validation error: step ", fmt_step(best_step), " ")) + scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 8000), labels = scales::label_comma()) + labs(x = "Gradient-descent step (log scale)", y = "Mean squared error", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A network with 40 hidden units trained for 8,000 steps. Training error falls throughout. Validation error is lowest at step 1,937 and then rises.](training-a-network_files/figure-html/fig-early-stopping-1.png){#fig-early-stopping fig-alt='Two curves of mean squared error against gradient-descent steps on a log scale. Both start high, training at 1.001 and validation at 1.090, and fall together. The training curve keeps falling, to 0.540 at step 8,000. The validation curve reaches its lowest point, 0.564, at step 1,937, where a dashed vertical line is drawn, then turns upward to 0.589, leaving a widening gap.' width=1500} ::: ::: Training error falls from 1.001 to 0.540 and is still falling at the end. Validation error is lowest at step 1,937, at 0.564, and rises to 0.589 by step 8,000, 4% worse. After step 1,937 the network is learning the training stations' noise. **Early stopping** keeps the weights from the step where validation error was lowest; here it also saves 76% of the steps. Early stopping is a form of regularisation. The weights start small, and a network with small weights is close to linear; training grows them. Stopping early limits how far they grow, which is what the ridge penalty of [Regularisation](../05-generalisation/regularisation.qmd) does directly. ### The random start changes the score Ten networks with eight hidden units are trained the same way, differing only in the seed that draws their starting weights. Averaging their predictions gives an eleventh model. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} seed_runs <- map(1:10, \(seed) train(initialise(seed, 8), learning_rate = 0.2, steps = 3000)) seed_mse <- map_dbl(seed_runs, \(run) last(run$validation)) averaged <- map(seed_runs, \(run) forward(run$par, X_valid)$prediction) |> reduce(`+`) / length(seed_runs) averaged_mse <- mean((y_valid - averaged)^2) tibble(Model = c("Best single network", "Worst single network", "Average of all ten"), `Validation MSE` = round(c(min(seed_mse), max(seed_mse), averaged_mse), 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Model | Validation MSE| |:--------------------|--------------:| |Best single network | 0.526| |Worst single network | 0.580| |Average of all ten | 0.548|
::: ::: The ten networks share the data, the settings and the number of steps, yet their validation MSE spans 0.055. That is the seed alone: a network's loss has many valleys, and each start rolls into a different one. Averaging the ten networks' predictions scores 0.548, better than seven of the ten single networks, the same idea as the many trees of [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd). Fit a network several times from different seeds and report the spread, as [Uncertainty and stability](../07-validation/uncertainty-and-stability.qmd) does for any model. On this survey, a difference between two networks smaller than 0.055 could be the seed alone. ## Large datasets are trained in mini-batches Every step on this page uses all 541 training stations to compute the slopes. With hundreds of thousands of rows that is slow, so large networks are trained on **mini-batches**: the rows are shuffled and split into small groups, say of 32, and each step uses one group. This is the **stochastic gradient descent** that [Gradient descent](../04-how-algorithms-learn/gradient-descent.qmd) named. Each step's slopes are then a noisy estimate, but they cost a fraction of the time, and the noise evens out over many steps. One pass through all the groups is an **epoch**, the usual unit for how long a network trains. ## `mlp()` takes the settings as arguments In tidymodels a network is specified with `mlp()`, a multilayer perceptron, the usual name for the networks on these pages. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} network <- mlp(hidden_units = 8, penalty = 0.01, epochs = 500) |> set_engine("nnet") |> set_mode("regression") network_data <- mutate(model_data, log_abundance = log1p(abundance)) network_recipe <- recipe( log_abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3, data = network_data) |> step_log(chlorophyll_mg_m3, offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) set.seed(6) fitted_network <- workflow(network_recipe, network) |> fit(data = network_data[-validation, ]) mlp_predictions <- augment(fitted_network, network_data[validation, ]) mlp_mse <- mean((mlp_predictions$log_abundance - mlp_predictions$.pred)^2) tibble(`Validation MSE` = round(mlp_mse, 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Validation MSE| |--------------:| | 0.597|
::: ::: With a small penalty and no early stopping, this network scores 0.597, behind the averaged networks above; the second exercise below tries other penalties. `step_normalize()` standardises the inputs, and `penalty` is the ridge penalty on the weights. `hidden_units` and `penalty` take `tune()` and are chosen by cross-validation, as [How much data a network needs](how-much-data.qmd) does. `epochs` means something slightly different here: the `nnet` engine does not use gradient descent but BFGS, the search described on [Forward propagation and backpropagation](forward-and-backward.qmd), so it has no learning rate, and `epochs` sets its maximum number of iterations (`maxit`). It still says how long to search. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The maths, if you want it Each step of gradient descent moves every weight $w$ against its slope, $w \leftarrow w - \eta \, \partial L / \partial w$, where $\eta$ is the learning rate. With mini-batches, $L$ is the loss on one batch $B$ of rows, $L_B = \frac{1}{|B|} \sum_{i \in B} (y_i - \hat y_i)^2$, so every step sees a different batch. A ridge penalty $\lambda$ adds $\lambda \sum w^2$ to the loss, and the step becomes $w \leftarrow w - \eta \, (\partial L / \partial w + 2 \lambda w)$: every step also pulls each weight a little towards zero. Early stopping limits the same growth by limiting the number of steps. ::: ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Three settings decide how a network trains: the **learning rate**, the **number of steps** and the **random starting weights**. - The learning rate trades speed for stability: here 0.2 went lowest, 0.5 bounced around the valley floor and 2 became `NaN` without a warning. Look at the curve, not only the final number. - **Early stopping** keeps the weights from the step where validation error is lowest, here step 1,937 of 8,000. It restrains the weights as a penalty does. - Ten runs differing only in their seed varied by 0.055 in validation MSE. Report the spread across seeds, or average several networks. - Standardise the inputs, and train on large datasets in **mini-batches**; an **epoch** is one pass through all of them. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Re-run the learning-rate sweep with 16 hidden units instead of 4. Does 0.2 still go lowest, or does the larger network need a smaller rate? 2. Change `penalty` in `mlp()` to 0 and then to 1. Which gives the lowest validation MSE, and how does it compare with the averaged networks?
